creative_rules: no book cover in the Pin artwork
no sales copy in the artwork
visual concept must match the guide problem rather than look like a generic AI illustration
status_note: Copy, landing pages, UTM structure and creative briefs are ready. Scheduling in Metricool requires one compliant image and a Pinterest board for each Pin.

pins.title: What to Do When Your Child Gets Angry After Losing
pins.description: Losing can feel enormous to a child. Start with connection, lower the pressure, and help them find a next step after the big feeling passes. Free parent guide from Emma Bellori Books.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn scene of a child pausing after a board game while a caring adult offers calm support.
pins.creative_brief: Quiet post-game scene, pieces still on table, child visibly frustrated but not caricatured, adult nearby at child level; warm editorial watercolor/pencil feel.

pins.title: How to Teach Kids Good Sportsmanship Without a Lecture
pins.description: Good sportsmanship grows through tiny repeated habits: fair play, kind endings, repair after frustration and trying again. Use these practical ideas at home.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn children ending a game with a friendly gesture after playing together.
pins.creative_brief: Two children after a tabletop or playground game, one offering a small friendly gesture; show mixed emotions and warmth, not trophy imagery.

pins.title: Low-Pressure Games That Help Kids Practice Losing
pins.description: Children can practice disappointment in small, safe doses. These playful ideas make winning and losing less emotionally loaded without forcing a perfect reaction.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn family playing a simple tabletop game with relaxed expressions and colorful pieces.
pins.creative_brief: Cozy family tabletop scene, simple homemade game pieces, imperfect natural gestures, no branded board game.

pins.title: How to Help a Child Who Is Afraid to Make Mistakes
pins.description: When fear of being wrong stops a child from trying, make the first step smaller and turn mistakes into useful information. Four practical ways to help.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn child hesitating over a creative project while an adult calmly supports the first small step.
pins.creative_brief: Child at desk with unfinished drawing/building project, pencil hovering, adult beside rather than over them; expressive hands and natural clutter.

pins.title: When Your Child Wants Everything to Be Perfect
pins.description: Careful work can be a strength. But when “good” only feels acceptable if it is flawless, these everyday strategies can make trying and finishing feel safer.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn child comparing two imperfect drawings and learning to leave one finished.
pins.creative_brief: Two drawings side by side, eraser crumbs, child considering rather than distressed; emphasize process and tactile paper texture.

pins.title: A 3-Step Growth Mindset Routine After a Mistake
pins.description: Skip the slogans. Help children notice what happened, choose one useful change, and decide when to try again with this simple routine.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn child rebuilding a block structure after noticing why it fell.
pins.creative_brief: Block tower partly fallen with child calmly testing a different base; show observation and adjustment, not a celebratory success pose.

pins.title: What to Say When Your Child Says “I Can’t Do It”
pins.description: “I can’t” can mean the task feels hard, the first step is unclear, or failure feels risky. Try these calm responses instead of arguing or over-reassuring.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn adult and child looking together at a difficult puzzle and choosing one small next step.
pins.creative_brief: Adult and child side by side with puzzle/craft, one small piece highlighted by composition; collaborative rather than instructional posture.

pins.title: How to Help a Child Join a Game With Other Kids
pins.description: Joining play has hidden steps: watch, notice what the group is doing, choose a useful opening and handle either yes or no. Practice them gently at home.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn playground scene where one child watches a group game before finding a natural way to join.
pins.creative_brief: Playground or park, small group building/chalking/ball play, observing child at edge but visually connected; avoid sad isolated stereotype.

pins.title: When Your Child Says “No One Wants to Play With Me”
pins.description: Before solving the friendship problem, help your child feel heard and understand what actually happened. Then choose one practical next move together.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn child talking with a parent after a difficult friendship moment, with gentle attentive body language.
pins.creative_brief: After-school conversation on bench/sofa, backpack nearby, child explaining while adult listens; intimate editorial scene, no melodrama.

pins.title: 4 Friendship Role-Play Games for Kids
pins.description: Practice invitations, kind refusals, disagreement and repair before the playground moment matters. Four short role-play games families can try at home.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn children using toys for a playful friendship role-play activity at home.
pins.creative_brief: Two children or child/adult using simple figures/puppets to rehearse a social scene; warm floor-level play, subtle humor.

pins.title: How to Support a Child After Friend Rejection
pins.description: A friend saying no can feel much bigger than the moment itself. Help your child separate what happened from what they fear it means, then decide whether action is needed.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn child processing a friendship disappointment with calm support nearby.
pins.creative_brief: Reflective scene after social disappointment, perhaps child drawing or sitting with caregiver; hopeful negative space, no crying close-up.

pins.title: A Simple Bedtime Routine for More Independent Sleep
pins.description: Independent sleep does not have to begin with a sudden separation. Use a short, predictable routine and change one small step at a time.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn cozy bedtime scene with a child following a simple visual routine before sleep.
pins.creative_brief: Warm bedroom, 3–4 visual routine cues in environment, parent and child near final story step; soft pencil/watercolor, not overly dreamy.

pins.title: How to Build Bedtime Independence Gradually
pins.description: Think of bedtime independence as a ladder, not a jump. Start from what happens now, make one understandable change, and repeat before moving on.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn bedtime scene showing a parent sitting a little farther from the child’s bed as part of a gradual routine.
pins.creative_brief: Bedroom composition with chair positioned near but not at bedside; child settled with comfort object; visual storytelling of gradual distance.

pins.title: 7 Screen-Free Calming Activities Before Bed
pins.description: Choose one or two quiet activities that are easy to stop and repeat. Here are seven simple screen-free ideas for the transition into bedtime.
pins.alt: Hand-drawn collection of calm bedtime activities including a book, drawing paper, stuffed animal and gentle stretching.
pins.creative_brief: Editorial collection scene rather than infographic: open book, small drawing, stuffed animal, child stretching in cozy room; tactile objects and hand-drawn imperfections.
